The whole combined refugee/IDP module of the revised instrument, with the customisations from the two cards above carried into it. These are drafts for review, not enumerator text. The naming rule throughout: name where the claim is lodged, never who adjudicates it — eligibility panels, appeals boards and hotlines are excluded even where they are well known, because a respondent never went near them.

The office doesn't travel everywhere. In many countries the claim is lodged online, by post, at a police station, or happens automatically with no office a respondent would visit — those are flagged above with the actual channel, so the wording can be adapted rather than asked as written.

Confidence is HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW per country. LOW rows are almost entirely small Pacific and Caribbean states; check MEDIUM and LOW against a country source before fielding.

Cross-checked against UNHCR’s internal Registration Baseline Survey (2024/25). Where the operation itself answered, the note under the module records what it said — joint, parallel or split registration, the year registration was handed over to the Government, which document types UNHCR issues — and flags the handful of countries where its answer doesn’t match the office named here. It also adds 29 countries the public scrape never covered, with the registrar known but no office or document named yet (LOW confidence).

Internal displacement is deliberately absent. Of the major contexts checked, only a handful have a verifiable IDP status document; most have none at all, which is a finding about the instruments, not a gap in the search.

Read this before using any of it

These are drafts for review, not enumerator text — translations are unreviewed, actor names are UCDP’s not a respondent’s, and identity groups are never named.

These are drafts for review, not enumerator text.

The translations are unreviewed. Translating an instrument is a specialist job — TRAPD, or forward-and-back translation with reconciliation — because a question has to be understood the same way, not merely mean the same thing. Cognitive testing on an unreviewed translation tests the translation, not the question.

“Flee” is rendered as leaving under duress, not fleeing in panic. The item defines it as leaving “due to events that posed a threat”, so the sense is compelled departure. Five of these languages have a default verb that instead means running away in fear — fuir, huir, الفرار, спасаясь бегством, 逃离 — and each of those invites a respondent to picture a panicked escape and answer “no” if their own departure was deliberate: packing over days, or leaving after a threat rather than during an attack. That is exactly the population these questions exist to count. All five now use a duress construction.

Still open: persecution, a legal term of art in the refugee definition that in everyday registers reads as ordinary harassment — a materially different threshold, and not something an automatic process can settle.

The names are UCDP’s, not a respondent’s. UCDP writes “JAS” where a Nigerian respondent says Boko Haram. Actor names are never translated — they are proper nouns.

Identity groups are never named. UCDP codes communal violence as, for example, “Christians (Nigeria) – Muslims (Nigeria)”, and at subnational level as named ethnic groups. Correct as conflict coding, unusable in an instrument a government enumerator reads aloud. Those become “communal or intercommunal violence”.

Naming actors risks anchoring. Someone displaced by a group not named may conclude the option does not cover them. Category phrasing is preferred where the data allows, and every example is tagged with which it is.

Subnational sets appear only where they say something different. A region whose examples merely repeat the national list is not shown.

Sources: UCDP GED for conflict, IDMC for hazards. Generated by prototype-python/build_questions.py. Ctrl/Cmd-P prints the form alone.
